elimination-diet.text: Appearance communities use elimination diets to hunt for foods that set off acne or flare-ups, then reintroduce them one at a time to confirm. The method is established for diagnosing food allergy; trials on finding skin triggers are limited.

low-histamine-diet.text: Users follow it to reduce facial flushing, redness and eczema-type skin symptoms they attribute to histamine. Followers favour fresh food and limit aged, fermented and cured items. The histamine-intolerance concept and its skin benefits are thinly studied.

chain: Whole foods, no grains or dairy
paleo-diet.text: Followers adopt paleo eating for a leaner physique and for less inflammation, built on meat, vegetables, fruit and nuts. Short trials report some metabolic changes; evidence for body composition and long-term appearance outcomes is limited.

whole30.text: People use Whole30 as a one-month reset, aiming for a leaner body, better energy and clearer skin, then reintroduce foods to spot personal triggers. Gains are mostly reported anecdotally; the program has no controlled trials of its own.

bryan-johnson-blueprint-diet.text: Looksmaxxers follow Bryan Johnson's published meal plan as part of a longevity routine aimed at slowing biological aging and keeping a youthful look. The evidence is his own tracked biomarkers; the diet has not been trialled in others.

longevity-blue-zones-diets.text: Users copy the eating patterns of long-lived regions in the hope of staying lean and looking younger for longer. The link to youthful skin is drawn from population observation, and the underlying longevity data are disputed.

orange-juice-vitamin-c-diet.text: Users drink orange juice or take large amounts of vitamin C to support collagen and brighten skin. The collagen role of vitamin C is established; high-intake effects on appearance specifically are untested.

cinnamon-apple-cider-vinegar-shots.text: Home-made apple cider vinegar shots, sometimes with cinnamon, are taken to reduce bloating, aid fat loss and clear skin. These appearance claims are based largely on anecdote, with no high-quality trials behind them.

fat-burner-supplements.text: Users take multi-ingredient stimulant blends to speed fat loss and get a leaner, more defined look. Efficacy has not been established at the category level, and blends vary widely between products.

green-tea-egcg.text: Green tea and EGCG extracts are used as a mild fat-burner to help get leaner. Support comes mostly from lab and animal studies, with human appearance outcomes less established.

vitamin-a-retinyl-palmitate-from-liver.text: Diet communities eat liver or take liver-derived products as a source of preformed vitamin A, aiming for better skin. Vitamin A's role in skin is well known through retinoids; appearance trials of dietary liver have not been run.

cod-liver-oil.text: Users take cod liver oil for its vitamin A, vitamin D and omega-3 content, hoping for better skin and general health. Its nutrients are well characterised; appearance outcomes have not been trialled.

chain: Claimed support for bone and teeth
fermented-cod-liver-oil-butter-oil-westo.text: Followers of the Weston A. Price Foundation take this pairing as a source of fat-soluble vitamins, aiming for dental, skeletal and facial-structure benefits. The facial-structure link is a theory with no clinical studies.

chain: Traditional foods, no refined flour or sugar
Claimed better dental and jaw development
weston-a-price-diet.text: Proponents follow this traditional-foods diet based on a 1930s dentist's comparisons of teeth and facial development, believing it supports facial structure and fewer cavities. The diet itself has not been trialled for appearance.

ray-peat-diet.text: Followers eat milk, fruit, juice and saturated fats to raise metabolism and correct hormone balance, aiming for a leaner, healthier look. Support comes from Peat's writings and anecdote; there are no trials.

chain: Cut seed oils, nuts, fatty fish
low-pufa-diet.text: Ray Peat followers avoid polyunsaturated fats on the theory that they oxidise and burden metabolism, hoping for better skin and body composition. The idea is untested as an appearance strategy.

anti-estrogen-diet-cruciferous-dim.text: Users in T-optimization circles eat broccoli and similar vegetables or take DIM to lower estrogen activity and raise the testosterone-to-estrogen ratio for a leaner, more masculine look. No trial in men shows a visible change.

chain: Support for muscle and masculine features
testosterone-boosting-diet-eggs-oysters-.text: Looksmaxxing and fitness circles eat these foods to support testosterone, muscularity and masculine features. Correcting nutrient deficiencies is known to matter; the diet has not been shown to raise testosterone in men who are already replete.

oysters-shellfish-for-zinc.text: Oysters are eaten as the richest food source of zinc, a mineral linked to testosterone production, to support muscle and masculine development. Benefit is tied to correcting a deficiency rather than boosting normal levels.

boron-zinc-d3-test-boost-stack.text: Supplement and looksmaxxing communities combine these three to raise testosterone for muscle and masculine looks. Each ingredient has some published link to hormone physiology, but the combination has no trial.

soy-avoidance.text: Fitness and looksmaxxing communities avoid soy out of concern that phytoestrogens lower testosterone or feminise men. Meta-analyses have found no effect of soy or isoflavones on male hormones.

plastic-endocrine-disruptor-avoidance.text: Users swap plastic for glass or steel and avoid certain packaging to protect testosterone and hormone balance. Regulators are tightening limits on these chemicals, but avoidance trials in men are absent.

tap-water-fluoride-avoidance.text: Some appearance-focused users drink and wash with filtered or spring water to avoid fluoride and chlorine, presenting it as part of a skin and health routine. Health bodies back fluoridation, critics dispute it, and no appearance data exist.

chain: Filter or spring water in place of tap
filtered-spring-water.text: Some people drink filtered or bottled spring water to avoid fluoride and chlorine, hoping for cleaner skin and general health. Tap water is heavily regulated and no appearance benefit has been documented.

alcohol-avoidance-sober-maxxing.text: Sober maxxers quit alcohol to get clearer, less puffy skin and better sleep. Alcohol's health effects are well documented; improvement in appearance after quitting has not been formally tested.

quitting-smoking-vaping.text: Appearance communities cite quitting to slow premature skin aging, since smoker's face brings a distinctive wrinkle pattern and sallow tone. Smoker's face is well documented; how much of it reverses after quitting is thinly studied.

caffeine-avoidance.text: Users cut caffeine hoping for less facial puffiness and better sleep, which they link to a fresher look. Caffeine's effects on sleep are documented; the effect on puffiness is untested.

coffee-for-skin-cold-brew.text: Appearance communities promote coffee and cold brew, drunk or applied topically, for skin and looks. General health data on coffee exist; the skin claims are untested.

chain: Supports skin, hair and nail cells
nutritional-yeast-b-vitamin-loading.text: Users eat fortified nutritional yeast or stack B-complex in the hope of better skin, hair and nails. The vitamins' roles are established, but their cosmetic payoff beyond correcting a deficiency is unstudied.

heavy-cream-butter-diet.text: Appearance communities use this high-fat dairy variant of low-carb eating to lose fat and keep meals simple. It has not been trialled for looks.
